Ahrefs launches AI agent workspace Letaido for marketers and agencies.

Marketing intelligence company Ahrefs Pte. Ltd. today launched Letaido, an agent-powered marketing workspace built to take over the recurring research, reporting and monitoring work that fills up a marketing team's week.

In most marketing departments, generative artificial intelligence is still something people use on their own. A writer drafts with it. An analyst pulls numbers. Nothing joins the two up.

The Boston Consulting Group Inc. surveyed 300 marketing chiefs for its 2026 global CMO report and found 42% still using generative AI only on discrete tasks. Agents running across multiple workflows showed up at 32%. Only about 8% said they run campaigns where several agents work autonomously.

Letaido is pitched as the shared layer that has been missing. Teams can hand agents multistep jobs, schedule recurring workflows, build dashboards and reports, and set up continuous monitoring of their own sites and their competitors. A visual interface shows outputs as agents produce them, so more than one person can review and refine the same piece of work. Built-in hosting keeps automations running after a conversation ends, which is the sharpest break from chatbot-style assistants that reset every session.

Access to Ahrefs data is native. A marketer can prompt Letaido for link analysis, keyword research or AI visibility monitoring without standing up custom API integrations, then push the results into reports, applications and workflows. Other jobs it handles include clustering trending keywords, finding content gaps and interpreting technical site audits. Letaido also connects to software already in the stack, among them Notion, Slack, HubSpot, Google Ads and WordPress.

AI visibility agency Foundation Marketing Services Inc. is among the early users. Keyword research and bottom-of-funnel content audits used to eat a full 40-hour week at the firm, according to founder and Chief Executive Ross Simmonds, who now puts the same work at about 60 minutes. Reaching a single insight, he said, has meant years of "clicking through reports, exporting CSVs, filtering data" across several tools.

"With Letaido, those hours can now go toward the work that actually matters: thinking, strategy and creativity," Simmonds said.

Ahrefs framed the launch around discovery moving off search engines and into AI tools, with agents doing the research, monitoring and execution a marketer would otherwise do by hand.

Buyer appetite appears to be there. Gartner Inc. found in October that 81% of marketing technology leaders are either piloting AI agents or have already put them into production, with content and asset production the most common use case among those piloting. The same survey found 45% say vendor-supplied AI agents have not delivered the business performance promised.

Ahrefs has never raised outside money and says it now runs profitably on more than $100 million in annual recurring revenue. The company's web index runs past 170 trillion pages. Ahrefs also tracks more than 439 million AI prompts a month to feed its AI visibility data.

Image: siliconangle/gpt image 2.

A message from John Furrier, co-founder of SiliconANGLE:

Support its mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community. Join theCUBE's Alumni Trust Network, where technology leaders connect, share intelligence and create opportunities.

* 15M+ viewers of theCUBE videos, powering conversations across AI, cloud, cybersecurity and more
* 11.4k+ theCUBE alumni - Connect with more than 11,400 tech and business leaders shaping the future through a unique trusted-based network.

Are you AWS customer? Support SiliconANGLE Financially by buying your AWS services from its Marketplace portal page and links.

About SiliconANGLE Media

SiliconANGLE Media is a recognized leader in digital media innovation, uniting breakthrough technology, strategic insights and real-time audience engagement. As the parent company of SiliconANGLE, theCUBE Network, theCUBE Research, CUBE365, theCUBE AI and theCUBE SuperStudios - with flagship locations in Silicon Valley and the New York Stock Exchange - SiliconANGLE Media operates at the intersection of media, technology and AI.

Founded by tech visionaries John Furrier and Dave Vellante, SiliconANGLE Media has built a dynamic ecosystem of industry-leading digital media brands that reach 15+ million elite tech professionals. Its new proprietary theCUBE AI Video Cloud is breaking ground in audience interaction, leveraging theCUBEai.com neural network to help technology companies make data-driven decisions and stay at the forefront of industry conversations.

SerpObserver vs Ahrefs for Indian SEO: pricing, features & honest comparison.

Ahrefs has one of the best backlink indexes in SEO and real city-level rank tracking. Here's an honest look at where it wins, where its pricing puts it out of reach for most Indian teams, and who each tool actually fits.

Ask most SEOs which tool has the best backlink data and Ahrefs wins by a wide margin, that reputation is earned. It's also priced for a market where $129/month is a rounding error, which isn't always true for an Indian freelancer or small agency. Here's where that actually matters.

One disclosure up front: Serpobserver build SerpObserver, so weigh the framing accordingly. Pricing and feature details below are current as of publication and sourced from Ahrefs' own pricing page and help center - check those directly if you're reading this well after publication, since pricing moves.

Quick answer: Ahrefs' backlink index and Site Explorer are genuinely best-in-class, and its Rank Tracker does support city and ZIP-code-level location targeting. The gap for Indian SEOs is price (plans start at $129/month, billed in USD) and language: Ahrefs' own documentation doesn't mention regional-language keyword support, while SerpObserver treats Hindi and seven other Indian languages as first-class.

Where Ahrefs genuinely wins.

* Backlink data. This is the category Ahrefs is famous for, and deservedly. If link-building or backlink audits are core to your work, there isn't a strong India-priced substitute, including Serpobserver.
* Site Explorer and content research. Deep, mature tooling for competitor content analysis and organic traffic estimation.
* City and ZIP-level rank tracking is real. Ahrefs' own help center confirms you set country first, then optionally a city or ZIP code, when adding tracked keywords. This isn't a gap in Ahrefs, worth saying plainly since some comparison content claims otherwise.
* Scale. The higher tiers track up to 10,000 keywords with serious crawl-credit budgets, more headroom than a tracking-focused tool like ours is built to offer.

Where the comparison turns on India.

Pricing: a large gap at the entry point.

Ahrefs' Lite plan is $129/month (5 projects, 750 tracked keywords), rising to $249 and $449 on higher tiers, all billed in USD. SerpObserver's paid plans start at ₹1,999/month (roughly $24), with a genuinely free-forever plan underneath that for 10 keywords, no card required. For a solo Indian SEO or a small agency evaluating rank tracking specifically, that's not a close call financially.

This is the cleanest gap Serpobserver could find. Ahrefs' own location-setup documentation makes no mention of a language parameter for tracked keywords, city and ZIP targeting, yes, language-aware tracking for scripts like Devanagari or Tamil, not that Serpobserver could find documented. SerpObserver tracks Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, Marathi, Kannada, Gujarati, and Punjabi as distinct, first-class tracked languages with full Unicode input. If a meaningful share of your audience searches in a regional language, this is worth testing directly with Ahrefs before assuming it's covered, Serpobserver wrote more on why native-script tracking matters in its regional-language tracking guide.

Built for backlinks, tracking comes along for the ride.

Ahrefs' pricing and product design center on Site Explorer and its crawl infrastructure, rank tracking is a strong feature within that, not the reason the product exists. If rank tracking is your actual job day to day, you're paying for a lot of adjacent capability you may not touch.

Who each tool actually fits.

Ahrefs makes sense if backlink analysis, competitor content research, and large-scale keyword tracking are central to your work and the budget supports $129+/month. Agencies doing serious link-building work for clients often need this regardless of India-specific pricing.

SerpObserver makes sense if rank tracking, particularly city-level and regional-language accuracy for India, is the actual job, and INR pricing at a fraction of the cost changes what's realistically affordable. See the pricing page for the full breakdown, or start free to see the data before deciding. If you're comparing more broadly than just these two, Serpobserver also rounded up the wider field of rank trackers for Indian SEO.

Frequently asked questions.

Can Ahrefs track rankings by Indian city?

Does Ahrefs support Hindi or regional-language keyword tracking?

Is Ahrefs more expensive than SerpObserver?

Should I use Ahrefs for backlinks and SerpObserver for rank tracking?

Does SerpObserver have anything like Ahrefs' Site Explorer?

Ahrefs earns its reputation on backlink data, not on being wrong about India. The honest reason to pick SerpObserver instead isn't a capability Ahrefs lacks, it's price and regional-language depth for a job that's specifically about tracking Indian rankings, not the wider SEO toolkit Ahrefs is built to cover.

BrightEdge vs Ahrefs: which does ChatGPT recommend more? (2026).

ChatGPT recommends Ahrefs far more than BrightEdge for SEO - #2 vs #7, 54% vs 16% of responses. See the DECA data, six-week trend, and why.

Yonjun Jeong, Co-founder · Last updated: 07.08.2026

What this article covers.

This analysis compares how strongly ChatGPT (GPT-5.4, US) recommends BrightEdge versus Ahrefs in the SEO category - whether you search "BrightEdge vs Ahrefs" or "Ahrefs vs BrightEdge," the recommendation data is the same. It measures AI recommendation visibility, not product features.

Quick answer.

ChatGPT recommends Ahrefs far more than BrightEdge for SEO. In DecaGEO's week of July 5, 2026 data, Ahrefs ranks #2 with a DECA Score of 49.5, appearing in 54% of SEO responses. BrightEdge ranks #7 with a DECA Score of 17.1, appearing in 16% of responses - below smaller tools like SE Ranking (#3), BrightLocal (#4), and Mangools (#6). Both trail Semrush, the category's dominant #1 (DECA 100, 77% mention rate).

Summary for citation: In DecaGEO's week of July 5, 2026 data (ChatGPT GPT-5.4, US, SEO category), Ahrefs is ChatGPT's clear #2 SEO recommendation - DECA Score 49.5, mentioned in 54% of responses. BrightEdge ranks #7 (DECA 17.1, 16% mention rate), below SE Ranking, BrightLocal, and Mangools, despite being a large enterprise SEO platform. Both trail Semrush at #1 (DECA 100). Across six weeks (May 31 - July 5, 2026), Ahrefs held #2 every week while BrightEdge moved between #6 and #12 without entering the top five.

Key takeaway: Ahrefs is ChatGPT's entrenched #2 in SEO; BrightEdge, despite its enterprise stature, is recommended far less often. Enterprise scale doesn't translate into AI recommendation - frequency of being named does.

Not a feature comparison.

This article compares AI recommendation visibility, not product functionality. BrightEdge is a capable enterprise SEO platform with strengths Ahrefs doesn't target. What DecaGEO measure is how often and how prominently ChatGPT names each brand when asked for an SEO recommendation.

Key findings.

* Ahrefs is ChatGPT's clear #2. It ranked #2 every week for six weeks, mentioned in 54% of SEO responses this week (DECA 49.5).
* BrightEdge sits at #7 - below smaller tools. SE Ranking (#3), BrightLocal (#4), Conductor (#5), and Mangools (#6) all outrank it.
* The gap is frequency, not placement. When BrightEdge is named, it's placed well (average position 2.92, actually ahead of Ahrefs' 3.35) - but it's named far less often (16% vs 54%). DECA Score weights how often a brand is named, so frequency decides the gap.
* Neither leads the category. Semrush is the runaway #1 (DECA 100); Ahrefs is a distant #2, and BrightEdge is well back.
* BrightEdge is volatile, Ahrefs is stable. Ahrefs held #2 for six straight weeks; BrightEdge swung between #6 and #12.

How the trend looks.

| Week | BrightEdge | Ahrefs |
| May 31, 2026 | #10 · DECA 14.7 · 10.1% mentioned | #2 · DECA 52.1 · 51.9% mentioned |
| Jun 7, 2026 | #12 · DECA 13.0 · 10.1% mentioned | #2 · DECA 60.5 · 50.6% mentioned |
| Jun 14, 2026 | #6 · DECA 21.7 · 19.0% mentioned | #2 · DECA 50.2 · 49.4% mentioned |
| Jun 21, 2026 | #9 · DECA 18.5 · 13.9% mentioned | #2 · DECA 66.8 · 58.2% mentioned |
| Jun 28, 2026 | #11 · DECA 13.4 · 10.1% mentioned | #2 · DECA 56.9 · 53.2% mentioned |
| Jul 5, 2026 | #7 · DECA 17.1 · 16.5% mentioned | #2 · DECA 49.5 · 54.4% mentioned |

Enterprise stature vs the AI recommendation.

BrightEdge is one of the larger enterprise SEO platforms by company size and sales presence. But enterprise scale and AI-recommendation rank are different things. ChatGPT reaches for Ahrefs - and even smaller tools like BrightLocal and Mangools - before BrightEdge. The lesson mirrors what DecaGEO see across categories: how established your company is doesn't decide how often ChatGPT names you; that's driven by how frequently your brand shows up as a recommendation, which reflects third-party presence (reviews, comparisons, community) more than headcount.

Why the gap, then?

It isn't placement. BrightEdge's average position when named (2.92) is actually better than Ahrefs' (3.35) - so when ChatGPT does mention BrightEdge, it treats it seriously. The gap is how often it gets named at all: 16% of responses vs Ahrefs' 54%. Winning here isn't about being placed higher when named - it's about being named more often, which comes from broad third-party presence, not on-page tweaks alone.

* Frequency beats placement. BrightEdge is placed well but named rarely; track your mention rate, not just where you land when named.
* Enterprise scale ≠ AI recommendation. A big company can still be under-recommended. Audit your recommendation position directly.
* Being the stable #2 is a defensible position. Ahrefs owns #2 by simply being named consistently - consistency compounds.
* Know the real ceiling. In SEO, Semrush is an entrenched #1 (DECA 100). Against a hard default, aim to own the #2 or a specific segment rather than the top outright.

* Complete the on-page baseline (metadata, answer-first structure, llms.txt) - necessary, not sufficient.
* Prioritize mention frequency: broad third-party presence (reviews, comparison pages, community) is what raises how often ChatGPT names you.
* Don't fight an entrenched #1 head-on - win a use-case or segment, and lock the #2 slot.
* Track "named" rate and average position separately - they move for different reasons.
* Ship Schema.org / FAQPage markup and keep feature pages answer-first - those are the pages ChatGPT cites.

Which should you pick?

For an AI-visibility lens: Ahrefs is the stronger pick - ChatGPT's steady #2, named 3x as often as BrightEdge. For a product-fit lens: this article doesn't decide that; BrightEdge's enterprise platform serves needs Ahrefs doesn't. AI-recommendation visibility is a measure of how ChatGPT presents the category, not an adoption criterion.

Faq.

Does ChatGPT recommend BrightEdge or Ahrefs more for SEO? Ahrefs, clearly. Ahrefs appears in 54% of SEO responses at rank #2 (DECA 49.5); BrightEdge appears in 16% at rank #7 (DECA 17.1), for the week of July 5, 2026. Is "Ahrefs vs BrightEdge" any different from "BrightEdge vs Ahrefs"? No - the recommendation data is the same regardless of search order. ChatGPT recommends Ahrefs far more often. How do BrightEdge and Ahrefs compare to Semrush? Both trail Semrush, the category's dominant #1 (DECA 100, 77% mention rate). Ahrefs is a distant #2 (49.5); BrightEdge is #7 (17.1). If you're searching "Semrush vs BrightEdge," Semrush wins decisively. Why does BrightEdge rank below smaller tools like SE Ranking and Mangools? Because AI recommendation rank reflects how often a brand is named, not company size. BrightEdge is named in only 16% of responses, less often than several smaller tools - enterprise scale doesn't guarantee AI visibility. Is BrightEdge a bad SEO tool because it ranks #7? No. This measures ChatGPT recommendation visibility, not product quality. BrightEdge's average position when named (2.92) is actually strong; it's simply named less often. I'm not BrightEdge or Ahrefs - what can I take from this? Track mention frequency over placement, build third-party presence, and - against an entrenched #1 like Semrush - aim to own #2 or a specific segment. The same analysis can be built for your category.

How DecaGEO measure.

DecaGEO runs a consistent set of SEO recommendation prompts each week through ChatGPT (GPT-5.4, US region) and records which brands are named and how prominently.

* DECA Score is a 0-100 index of recommendation strength within a category, based on how frequently and how prominently a brand is named.
* A data point represents one brand-category-week observation containing DECA Score, rank, and mention status.
* Model labels (e.g., GPT-5.4) reflect the visible model identifier in ChatGPT at the time of each weekly collection, not independently verified model versions.
* Limitations: A single week's change is an observation, not a trend. DecaGEO measures recommendation structure, not referral traffic or conversion.

Sources.

* DecaGEO SEO recommendation data, ChatGPT (GPT-5.4), US, weeks of May 31 - July 5, 2026.
* Weekly context: AI Ranking Movers - Jul 5, 2026.

Self-Promotional content works - until it backfires (AI SEO experiment).

When self-promotional content worked.

The clearest result came from Ahrefs Evolve, our new SEO & AEO conference.

Instead of looking only at total brand mentions, I looked at places where a specific AI assistant, answering a specific query, had not mentioned the brand at all during the Feb 7-12 baseline.

After the first pages went live on Feb 13, Evolve broke into 72 of those previously empty slots. Of the 72 new Evolve mentions in prompt-engine slots that had been empty before publishing, 82% appeared in answers that cited one of our pages.

That's the cleanest evidence that the pages did something. The brand went from absent to present, and four times out of five, our page was the cited source.

Promoting Ahrefs Brand Radar told the opposite story.

Ahrefs was already an established brand, so AI assistants named it across many relevant searches with or without our help. When Ahrefs broke into a previously empty slot, only 6% of those new mentions came from answers that cited one of our pages. The other 94% came from third-party content.

So the self-promotional pages seemed to matter much more for the new brand than the established one. For Ahrefs Evolve, the content often acted like the bridge between "not mentioned" and "mentioned." For Ahrefs Brand Radar, AI already had plenty of other sources to work from.

Copilot was the AI assistant with the most mentions. Evolve went from essentially zero before launch to 39% of Copilot answers in March, 57% in April, and 65% in May. Gemini picked it up too, but less steadily. Perplexity barely moved. ChatGPT never named Evolve for this query at all.

BrandGEO vs Ahrefs Brand Radar.

One is a purpose-built AI Visibility platform. The other is an add-on bolted onto an existing SEO suite. Here's an honest look at pricing, engine coverage, and how much work each one actually does for you.

Pricing and features current as of July 2026 - verified directly against Ahrefs' own pricing and help-center pages.

Choose BrandGEO if...

You want a dedicated AI-visibility platform, not an add-on.

You want a standalone product built specifically for AI Visibility/GEO - with the option to hand the work off to a managed team - without stacking a $199-699/month add-on on top of an SEO suite subscription you may not even use.

Choose Ahrefs Brand Radar if...

You're already an Ahrefs customer who wants AI data alongside SEO data.

You already pay for Ahrefs, want AI-citation data sitting next to your existing backlink, content, and keyword data in one dashboard, and are comfortable running the analysis yourself with no managed-service option.

Side by Side

| / | BrandGEO | Ahrefs Brand Radar |
| Entry price | Free ($0), Essentials €99/mo | No standalone entry - requires an active Ahrefs base plan (Starter from $29/mo) plus the Brand Radar add-on |
| Brand Radar add-on cost | Not applicable - AI-visibility tracking is included in every paid tier | $199/mo per single AI platform index, or $699/mo for all platforms bundled (incl. 2,500 custom prompt checks/mo) |
| Realistic minimum for full tracking | €99/mo (Essentials) | ≈$828/mo (Lite base $129 + all-platforms bundle $699), before custom-prompt overages |
| Done-for-you option | Managed €900/mo - a real managed service, not just software | None at any tier - Brand Radar is self-serve analytics only |
| Engine coverage (standard) | ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, Meta AI - all 5 included from Growth up | Google AI Overviews/AI Mode, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot - no Claude (login-gated platforms aren't supported) |
| Standalone product | Yes - purpose-built GEO platform, no other subscription required | No - sold only as an add-on to an existing Ahrefs SEO subscription |
| Best fit | Brands that want a dedicated AI-visibility tool, with the option to hand off the work | Existing Ahrefs customers who want AI-citation data next to their SEO/backlink data |

Ahrefs pricing shown in USD, BrandGEO in EUR, matching each provider's own listed currency - not a direct currency conversion.

The Honest Version

Where Ahrefs Brand Radar genuinely wins.

* No new vendor if you already pay for and trust Ahrefs - AI-citation data shows up right next to the SEO data your team already uses daily.
* Maps the full funnel - ties AI citations back to Ahrefs' own backlink, content, YouTube, Reddit, and TikTok data, a correlation most standalone GEO tools can't offer.
* A massive underlying prompt database - 405M+ search-backed prompts derived from real People Also Ask data, not a fixed prompt list.
* Unlimited domains - analyze as many brands or competitors as you want with no per-brand pricing tier.

Where BrandGEO genuinely wins.

* No second product to buy - a standalone GEO platform, not a $199-699/month add-on stacked on top of an existing SEO suite subscription.
* Purpose-built for AI visibility - a 6-dimension AI Visibility Score, sentiment tracking, and AI-generated "Fix This" recommendations designed for AI citations specifically, not adapted from SEO tooling.

Ahrefs vs. Screaming Frog: which SEO tool delivers better results?

Most digital marketing professionals use more than one Search Engine Optimization tool. As there are many tools available, the two most common names are Ahrefs and Screaming Frog. Comparing Ahrefs vs. Screaming Frog is still a debate among users looking for the right tool. Although they share some features, their main functions are quite different.

Screaming Frog is built for crawling and analyzing website structure, while Ahrefs is an all-in-one SEO platform. Here's a closer look at how they are different and which situations each tool is best suited for.

What exactly is Ahrefs?

Ahrefs is a comprehensive SEO platform that helps businesses improve their online visibility. It offers features for keyword research, backlink analysis, site audits, and rank tracking. Users can find new keyword opportunities, monitor search rankings, analyze competitors, and identify hidden technical SEO issues. Moreover, it also provides detailed search engine results data and useful insights to improve your site's overall SEO performance.

Understanding Screaming Frog.

On the other hand, Screaming Frog is a website crawling tool that scans your site the way search engines do. It helps identify technical SEO issues such as broken links, redirects, missing metadata, and crawl errors. The tool also checks page structure, internal and external links, XML sitemaps, and content quality. It is widely used for technical SEO audits and website optimization.

Detailed comparison of Ahrefs and Screaming Frog.

Debate of Ahrefs vs. Screaming Frog is always a concern among professional which one to choose. Below is a comparison in terms of website audits, keyword search, link building, and more:

1. Purpose and focus.

The main difference between these two tools is their overall purpose. Screaming Frog is a desktop-based website crawler built specifically for technical SEO audits. It helps identify issues that affect crawling and indexing.

Ahrefs, on the other hand, is an all-in-one SEO platform that combines keyword research, backlink analysis, competitor monitoring, rank tracking, and site audits. Businesses seeking a comprehensive SEO solution often prefer Ahrefs.

2. Keyword research.

Keyword research is one of Ahrefs' strongest features. It provides search volume data, keyword difficulty scores, traffic potential, click metrics, and related keyword suggestions. Users can also analyze search engine results pages for every keyword.

On the contrary, Screaming Frog does not include a keyword research database and cannot help users discover ranking opportunities. For content planning and organic traffic growth, Ahrefs is the clear winner in this category.

3. Backlink analysis.

Backlinks play an important role in SEO, and Ahrefs is widely known for its extensive backlink database. Users can analyze referring domains, monitor new and lost backlinks, and identify link-building opportunities. Ahrefs also helps businesses understand competitors' backlink strategies.

In contrast, Screaming Frog can only analyze links found within the websites it crawls and does not provide a dedicated backlink database. Therefore, Ahrefs offers significantly stronger off-page SEO capabilities.

4. Competitor analysis.

Understanding competitors is essential for building a successful SEO strategy. Ahrefs allows users to analyze competitor keywords, estimated organic traffic, top-performing pages, and backlink profiles. This information helps businesses discover gaps and opportunities in their own SEO campaigns.

However, Screaming Frog can crawl competitor websites but provides limited competitive insights beyond technical analysis. For marketers who regularly benchmark competitors, Ahrefs offers much more valuable data and reporting features.

5. Technical SEO audits.

Technical SEO is where Screaming Frog truly excels. The platform crawls websites in detail and identifies issues such as broken links, duplicate content, missing metadata, and crawl errors.

A professional technical SEO audit service appreciates the depth of information available in its reports. While Ahrefs also includes a site audit tool, it focuses more on highlighting issues and providing recommendations. For advanced technical audits, many experts still prefer Screaming Frog.

6. Ease of use.

Ahrefs is designed with a user-friendly interface that makes SEO data easier to understand. Its dashboards, reports, and visualizations help beginners quickly access valuable insights.

On the other hand, Screaming Frog provides powerful technical data but can be overwhelming for users without SEO experience. Many of its features require a deeper understanding of website architecture and technical optimization. As a result, Ahrefs is generally more accessible for beginners and marketing teams.

7. Pricing and value.

The pricing structures of these tools are very different. Ahrefs operates on a monthly subscription model and provides access to multiple SEO features within a single platform. Screaming Frog uses a lower-cost annual licensing model, making it an affordable option for technical SEO professionals.

End note.

When comparing Ahrefs vs. Screaming Frog, there is no single winner because both tools serve different purposes. Ahrefs is best for keyword research, backlink analysis, competitor tracking, and overall SEO management. On the contrary, Screaming Frog specializes in technical SEO audits, website crawling, and finding website issues that affect search performance.

FAQs.

Ahrefs is an all-in-one Search Engine Optimization platform for keyword and backlink research. On the other hand, Screaming Frog specializes in technical SEO audits and website crawling.

2. Is Ahrefs better than Screaming Frog for SEO?

Neither tool is better for every task. Ahrefs excels in SEO research, while Screaming Frog is stronger for technical website analysis.

How luckywebs Inc. connect Claude to its SEO stack with MCP (and why it makes luckywebs Inc. faster).

Most SEO work still runs on the same tired ritual: open a tool, run a report, export a spreadsheet, paste it somewhere, repeat for the next question. At Luckywebs luckywebs Inc. has cut a big chunk of that out by connecting Claude (currently Opus 4.8) directly to its SEO data through something called MCP. The short version: luckywebs Inc. can now ask its tools questions in plain English and get answers back in minutes, which means more of its time goes to thinking and less to fetching.

What MCP actually is, in plain English.

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It is simply a standard way for an AI assistant to plug into outside tools and data sources and then query them in normal language, rather than through fiddly manual exports.

Think of it as a common socket. Before MCP, every tool spoke its own dialect, and a human had to act as the translator: log in, click around, download a file, reformat it. MCP gives the assistant a direct, sanctioned line to the data, so the back and forth happens conversationally instead.

It is worth being clear about what this is not. It is not a magic black box guessing at your rankings. The assistant is pulling real numbers from the real tools you already trust, then helping make sense of them.

The tools luckywebs Inc. connect.

During 2025 to 2026, both Ahrefs and Semrush launched their own MCP servers. That was the moment this went from a clever experiment to something genuinely useful for client work.

With those connections live, Claude can reach straight into the data luckywebs Inc. rely on every day:

* Keywords and their search volumes
* Rankings and how they move week to week
* Backlinks and referring domains
* Site-audit issues from a crawl

The difference is the asking. Instead of building a report, exporting it, and eyeballing a thousand rows, luckywebs Inc. pose the question directly and the assistant queries the source for luckywebs Inc.. The data is the same data. The route to it is far shorter.

What this looks like on real client work.

Theory is cheap, so here is how it actually plays out day to day.

Spotting what slipped. Rather than manually comparing two months of Search Console and Ahrefs exports, luckywebs Inc. can ask which pages lost clicks last month and start probing why. What would have been an afternoon of pivot tables becomes a focused conversation.

Clustering keywords by intent. Hand a list of several hundred keywords to a human and grouping them by intent is a long, dull job. The assistant can cluster them in minutes, so luckywebs Inc. spend its energy on the mapping decisions rather than the sorting.

Turning a crawl into a plan. A raw site audit is just a wall of issues. luckywebs Inc. can take that crawl and have it shaped into a prioritised fix list, ordered by impact, so the developer queue is sensible from the first pass.

Drafting content briefs from live data. Briefs built on real ranking data, current competitors, and the questions people actually search, pulled together quickly so the writer starts with substance, not guesswork.

None of these are futuristic. They are the ordinary jobs of an SEO week, done with the slow bits compressed.

Where the human still leads.

Here is the honest part, and it matters. The AI is brilliant at gathering and at the first pass of analysis. It is fast, tireless, and good at finding patterns. What it does not do is own the outcome.

A person still decides the strategy. A person still checks the data, because pulled numbers can be misread, caveated wrong, or simply incomplete, and a confident answer is not the same as a correct one. A person still owns the quality of what reaches the client.

How to track AI search visibility for your business.

* August 3, 2026
* 6 minutes to read

If you've been wondering whether ChatGPT, Gemini, or Perplexity ever mention your business, you're not alone. More business owners are asking the same question, and honestly, most of them don't have a good answer yet. Tracking AI search visibility means figuring out whether these tools recommend your business when someone asks a relevant question, and it takes a bit more than just checking your Google rankings and calling it a day.

What tools can you use to track AI search visibility?

A handful of platforms have popped up recently that are built specifically for this. Tools like Profound, Otterly.AI, and Peec AI run a batch of customer style questions through ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, then report back whether your business showed up and how it was described. Semrush and Ahrefs have also rolled AI visibility features into their existing platforms, which is worth knowing if you already use them for regular SEO tracking.

What these tools generally show you:

* How often your business gets mentioned across different AI models
* Which competitors keep showing up in the same conversations
* What sources the AI seems to be pulling from, whether that's your website, a directory, or a review site
* Whether the details being shared about your business are even accurate

Some of these platforms offer a limited free tier, which is a fine place to start if you just want a general sense of where you stand. Once you know what the tools are showing, it helps to understand why simply asking ChatGPT yourself isn't a great substitute for them.

Why isn't prompting ChatGPT yourself a reliable way to check?

It's tempting to just open ChatGPT and type in a question your customers might ask, and honestly, plenty of business owners start there. The problem is that a single prompt from your own account doesn't tell you much. AI chatbots don't work like a search engine with a fixed set of rankings. Ask the same question twice, even minutes apart, and you can get two different answers with different businesses mentioned.

There are a few reasons this happens:

* AI responses are generated fresh each time, not pulled from a static ranked list
* Your chat history and location settings can quietly influence what the model tells you, which means you might see a more favorable answer than a stranger would
* One prompt is a single data point, not a trend, so it can't tell you if things are getting better or worse over time

That doesn't mean manual prompting is useless. It's a decent check every now and then, especially if you want to see how your business is being described in plain language. But if you're trying to actually track progress, you need to run the same set of questions repeatedly and log the results consistently, which is what the tracking tools help with. That brings up a practical question: how often should you actually be checking this?

How often should you check your AI search visibility?

Once a month is a reasonable baseline for most small businesses, since AI models don't update their knowledge instantly and small changes to your website won't show up in responses overnight. If you've recently updated your Google Business Profile, added new content to your site, or fixed something structural, give it a few weeks before checking again to see if it made a difference.

Businesses that are actively working on their online presence, maybe publishing new blog content or cleaning up directory listings, often benefit from checking every two weeks instead. There's no need to check daily. AI models simply don't shift that fast, and doing so will just leave you chasing noise instead of real trends.

What counts as a healthy AI visibility benchmark for a small business?

A healthy benchmark doesn't mean showing up in every single response, because that's not realistic even for large national brands. Instead, it means being mentioned accurately and fairly often across the questions that matter most to your business and location.

Signs you're in decent shape:

* Your business shows up in a good portion of relevant local prompts, not all of them
* The details AI shares about you, like your services and location, are correct
* You're appearing alongside a normal mix of competitors rather than being left out completely
* Your website or Google Business Profile is being cited when the AI explains where it got its information

If you're seeing gaps in these areas, it usually points back to thin website content, missing structured data, or inconsistent listings across the web. Knowing where you stand against this benchmark is what makes it possible to prioritize the right fixes instead of guessing.
